questions.text: Walk me through what happens when a user types a URL and presses enter. 🟢 Beginner · Must-know
questions.answer: (assuming https://example.com/dashboard) Parse and cache. The browser checks its own caches, then the OS resolver, then DNS. HTTPS is in the HSTS preload list or a prior response, so it goes straight to TLS rather than redirecting. TLS handshake. TCP three-way handshake, then TLS: client hello, server certificate, verification against the certificate store, key exchange, and session resumption via a ticket if one exists. This is expensive, and it is why connection reuse and session tickets matter. HTTP request. Under HTTP/2 or /3 the browser may coalesce requests on one connection. The request carries cookies, Accept, Accept-Encoding, User-Agent, and conditional headers. DNS to edge. Typically a CDN anycast address; TLS terminates at the edge, which serves from cache or forwards. Origin. The CDN forwards to an origin, usually a load balancer, which picks a target by least-connections or least-response-time, with health checks removing dead instances. Application. Middleware in a fixed order: helmet → CORS → request id → body parse → auth → rate limit → route → error handler. Data. The handler calls a service, which calls a repository: one query, one pooled connection, cached if appropriate. Response. Status, headers (Cache-Control, Vary, security headers, cookies), and a body, with compression negotiated via Accept-Encoding. Rendering. HTML parses; render-blocking CSS and parser-blocking JS are handled; first contentful paint; then hydration, then async chunks. Sub-resources and feedback. Images, fonts, deferred JS; hydration makes it interactive; an SPA route change then needs no network round trip.

questions.text: Explain the JavaScript event loop, microtasks, and why setTimeout(fn, 0) runs last. 🟢 Beginner · Must-know
questions.answer: JavaScript has one call stack and queues of work. The loop: take the next macrotask, run it to completion — draining the entire microtask queue after each task and after each microtask — render, then repeat. Macrotasks: setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI events, MessageChannel, postMessage. Microtasks: promise then/catch/finally, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver. So setTimeout(() => log(1), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => log(2)); log(3) prints 3, 2, 1: log(3) is synchronous, log(2) runs when the stack empties (before the next macrotask), and log(1) waits for a fresh tick. The delay is not magic — setTimeout(…, 0) enters a task queue, and nested timeouts are clamped to ~4ms after five levels.

questions.text: useEffect dependencies: what is compared, and what is the trap? 🟡 Intermediate · Must-know
questions.answer: The dependency array is compared element-wise with Object.is between renders. A length change always re-runs. No array means every render; an empty array means once after first render. The traps: Stale closures. [] closes over the first render's values forever. Fix: include what you read — or better, stop reading it. Use the functional updater (setState(prev => …)), a useRef for a value that should not retrigger, or move the read into the event handler. Objects and functions in the array. [{a: 1}] is a new object each render, so the effect re-runs every render. Memoise it, destructure the primitives you read, or compute inside. Development double-invocation. StrictMode intentionally mounts, unmounts, and remounts in development; a non-idempotent effect or a missing cleanup shows it. Fix: make every effect idempotent and clean it up properly, because production also remounts on Suspense boundaries and navigations. Effects that fetch on mount. Every caller must then guard. Prefer a data-fetching library that owns caching, or move the fetch to a route loader.

questions.text: When is an index not used? Give five reasons. 🟡 Intermediate · Must-know
questions.answer: A function or expression on the column. WHERE date(created_at) = '2026-01-01' cannot use a plain index. Fix: an expression index, or rewrite to a sargable range created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-01-02'. Implicit type conversion. WHERE user_id = '42' on an int column may cast the column. Match the parameter type. A leading wildcard. LIKE '%son' cannot use a B-tree. Fix: trigram or full-text index, or an exact prefix. The query returns a large fraction of rows. At 40% a sequential scan is cheaper than index lookups plus heap fetches; the planner is right, and "fixing" it makes it slower. A union branch whose type does not match the indexed column. The planner may take the branch without the index. (Bonus) Stale statistics. After a bulk load, ANALYZE has not run and estimates are wrong — a common cause of a "suddenly slow" query.

questions.text: Explain refresh token rotation with reuse detection. 🟡 Intermediate · Must-know
questions.answer: A 15-minute access token plus a long-lived refresh token in an httpOnly cookie. The access token can live in memory; the refresh token must not be readable by JavaScript.

questions.text: Explain the N+1 problem and three fixes. 🟢 Beginner · Must-know
questions.answer: Fetch 100 posts, then loop and fetch each author: 101 queries for one page. It is the most common ORM trap and usually invisible in development because per-query latency is low and the dataset is small. Three real fixes: Eager load / join. findMany({ include: { author: true } }) generates a join or a second batched query. Verify the generated SQL — that is the actual skill; read the query log. Batch. Extract ids, run one WHERE id IN (…), join in memory with a Map. Works without an ORM and is the safest general fix. DataLoader / a batching layer. For graph traversal it batches all loads for one event-loop tick into one query and caches per request, so a repeated lookup is free.

questions.text: What is idempotency, and where must it hold? 🔴 Advanced · Must-know
questions.answer: Performing an operation N times has the same effect as once. With at-least-once delivery, duplicates will happen, and the alternative is charging someone twice or sending two emails. Where it must hold, easiest to hardest: The API boundary. A client-supplied key persisted with a unique constraint. First request inserts; a retry gets a conflict and you return the *original response*, not an error. Essential for anything a client will retry. Your handlers. A job that runs twice must not send two emails: record the effect in the same transaction as the effect itself, keyed by an idempotency key, and return early on conflict. The external call. Pass a key to the provider (Stripe returns the original object on replay). Where a provider offers no idempotency, use a natural key — your id in their reference field, with a search before create. At-least-once consumers. ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING plus a unique constraint on the natural key.

questions.text: How do you run a schema migration with no downtime? 🔴 Advanced · Must-know
questions.answer: Run migrations as a separate one-off step *before* the new version serves traffic, guarded by an advisory lock, and make every migration backward-compatible with the version still running. That second half is what makes a rolling deploy safe, and it is the half people forget.

questions.text: Explain EXPLAIN ANALYZE output and how you read it. 🟡 Intermediate · Must-know
questions.answer: EXPLAIN shows the plan. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes and shows it with real timings and row counts, so never run it on a mutation outside a transaction you can roll back. Read in this order: Estimated versus actual rows per node, and the ratio. A 100× divergence means stale statistics or a predicate the planner did not model — ANALYZE may fix it, or the planner needs help. The loop. A nested loop re-executes the inner side per outer row. actual rows=1 inside an outer node of 500,000 is 500,000 index lookups. loops=. Per-loop cost times the loop count is the real cost. time=0.05 rows=1 loops=900000 is 45 seconds, and this is where people are surprised. Buffers: shared hit=… read=…. Reads are disk, hits are cache. High reads on a hot query mean the working set exceeds shared_buffers. Sort spills — Sort Method: external merge means it went to disk: fix the index or work_mem rather than raising work_mem globally. Node type. Seq Scan is not automatically bad on a small table. Index Only Scan is the target for read-heavy paths and needs a current visibility map or it still visits the heap.

questions.text: Explain retries and why naive retries are harmful. 🟡 Intermediate · Must-know
questions.answer: A naive retry is "try three times on failure". It fails for three reasons: not all failures are retryable (a 400 never succeeds; retrying a validation error is pure waste — retry only 429, 502, 503, 504, and connection errors, and only when the operation is idempotent or carries an idempotency key); retry storms (when a dependency degrades, every client retries at once, and the retries arrive just as it is recovering and knock it over again — this is how a 30-second blip becomes a 20-minute outage); and no jitter (without it, clients that failed together retry together in lockstep, forever).

questions.text: How do you debug a production issue with only logs? 🟡 Intermediate · Must-know
questions.answer: A method, not a vibe: Establish scope. All users, one tenant, one region, one endpoint, one version? Find a failing request id and search on it. If you cannot correlate, that is the finding — add correlation ids. Get a baseline. Error rate, p50/p95/p99, throughput, per-endpoint breakdown, saturation. A problem you cannot scope is usually a change: what deployed, what config moved, which dependency shifted behaviour. Form a falsifiable hypothesis. "The 502s started at 14:02, when the upstream certificate rotated" is testable; "something is wrong" is not. Narrow with data. Does it correlate with a version, tenant, region, status, flag, payload shape, or a particular country (timezones)? Bisect in time. Correlate the first error with deploys, config changes, status pages, and traffic shape. git bisect the deploy range if it looks like code. Reproduce locally with production-shaped data volumes — and say so honestly when a race needing 10k concurrent requests will not reproduce locally. Mitigate first, diagnose second. Roll back, disable a flag, shed load, fail over. The incident is not over until users are unblocked; root-causing during an outage is a privilege, not a duty. Then write it up. Timeline, impact, root cause, contributing factors, and the specific preventive change you shipped. Blameless — the target is the system, not the person.

questions.text: Explain database isolation levels with a concrete anomaly for each. 🟡 Intermediate · Must-know
questions.answer: Four anomalies, each assumed to arise from a transaction that reads then writes: Dirty read — reading uncommitted data. B reads A's uncommitted write; A rolls back; B acted on data that never existed. Postgres Read Committed does not permit this; MySQL InnoDB REPEATABLE READ does not either. Non-repeatable read — the same row read twice returns different values because another transaction committed between. Read Committed permits this, and that is what it means: each statement gets a fresh snapshot. Phantom read — a range query returns different row *sets* because rows were inserted. Postgres snapshot isolation does not permit phantoms within a statement, but two SELECT count(*) calls in one Read Committed transaction can differ. SERIALIZABLE prevents it. Write skew — two transactions read overlapping data, take different decisions, and both commit, breaking a joint invariant. Two on-call doctors each check "at least one is on shift", both see one, both go on break. Snapshot isolation permits it; SERIALIZABLE prevents it by aborting one with a serialization failure, which must be retried. | Level | Dirty | Non-repeatable | Phantom | Write skew | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Read Uncommitted | yes | yes | yes | yes | | Read Committed | no | yes | yes | yes | | Repeatable Read | no | no | mostly | yes | | Serializable | no | no | no | no |

practice.title: K.4 Rapid-Fire Bank
items: Foundations (1–20)
O(1) vs O(log n)? Array indexing is a fixed number of machine operations; a tree descent is one step per level, so it scales with height.
Why is binary search O(log n)? Each comparison halves the search space, so n → n/2 → n/4, reaching 1 in log₂(n) steps.
Amortized O(1) means? The total cost over n operations is O(n) even though individual operations can be O(n) — like doubling a dynamic array.
Hash table worst case? O(n) when all keys collide into one bucket; mitigated by chaining, tree-mode escalation, or randomization.
Stack vs heap allocation? Stack is LIFO, contiguous, automatic lifetime, fast; heap is dynamic, manual/GC lifetime, slower to access.
Process vs thread? A process has its own address space; threads share the heap and file descriptors but have their own stack and registers.
Race condition? Two threads access shared state without synchronization, producing a result dependent on interleaving.
Deadlock requires? Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait — break any one.
Mutex vs semaphore? A mutex is binary ownership of one resource; a semaphore is a counter allowing N concurrent holders.
TCP vs UDP? TCP gives ordered, reliable, congestion-controlled delivery; UDP is connectionless with no guarantees but no head-of-line blocking.
Why head-of-line blocking in TCP? Ordered delivery means a lost segment stalls all later data on the connection.
Three-way handshake? SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK — it synchronizes sequence numbers and establishes the connection state.
Time complexity of Python + on strings? O(n) per append because strings are immutable, so a loop is O(n²); use join.
Bit vs byte? A bit is one binary digit; a byte is 8 bits. Storage is measured in bytes; speed in bits per second.
Encoding vs encryption? Encoding is a reversible representation change (base64, UTF-8); encryption requires a key to reverse.
Big-O vs Big-Theta? Big-O is an upper bound; Big-Theta is a tight bound; Big-Omega is a lower bound.
Recursion → iteration? Use an explicit stack (or queue for BFS), which removes call-stack overhead and the depth limit.
Why is quicksort average O(n log n) and worst O(n²)? Partitioning is linear per level; worst-case pivots give n levels instead of log n.
In-place means? Constant extra space beyond the input — not necessarily O(1) time.
What is a hash collision and how do you handle it? Two keys map to the same bucket; handle by chaining (separate lists), open addressing with probing, or rehashing.
Frontend (21–45)
Event bubbling vs capturing? Events propagate target → ancestors (bubble) or window → target (capture); the bubble phase is the default handler phase.
What causes a reflow? Changing geometry-affecting properties (width, content, position) forces layout recomputation; read-then-write in a loop causes thrashing.
Event loop in the browser? macrotask queue (timers, I/O) → render opportunity → microtask queue (promises) drains completely first.
== vs ===? Loose uses type coercion (null == undefined is true); strict compares type and value.
null vs undefined? undefined means "no value assigned"; null means explicitly "no object/value".
Closure? A function plus the lexical environment it captured when created.
var in a loop with setTimeout? All callbacks see the final value because var is function-scoped; let creates a per-iteration binding.
Hoisting? Declarations are moved to the top of their scope; var becomes undefined, function declarations are initialized, let/const are in the temporal dead zone.
Promise.all vs allSettled? all resolves when all resolve and rejects on the first rejection; allSettled always waits and reports every outcome.
What is a microtask? A job in the microtask queue — promise callbacks and queueMicrotask — drained before the next macrotask.
useEffect dependency array? The values from render that the effect closes over; omitting one gives a stale closure, so include all or restructure.
Why key lists by id? React uses keys to decide which nodes to reuse; index keys misidentify nodes after reorder and corrupt state, focus, and animation.
What does React re-render mean? The component function re-runs and returns a new element tree; React then diffs and commits minimal DOM changes.
useMemo vs useCallback? useMemo caches a computed value; useCallback caches a function identity. Both are for referential stability or expensive work.
What is a render-prop vs hook? A render-prop is a function child receiving data; a hook is a function called inside a component that may use state and effects.
Context vs Redux/Zustand? Context propagates a value; a store adds subscriptions, selectors, and devtools, so only the components that read a slice re-render.
LCP, INP, CLS? Largest Contentful Paint (load), Interaction to Next Paint (responsiveness), Cumulative Layout Shift (visual stability).
How do you fix a large CLS? Reserve space for async content (width/height or aspect-ratio), avoid inserting content above existing content, use skeletons with exact dimensions.

questions.text: Walk me through what happens when a user types a URL and presses enter. 🟢 Beginner · Must-know
questions.answer: (assuming https://example.com/dashboard) Parse and cache. The browser checks its own caches, then the OS resolver, then DNS. HTTPS is in the HSTS preload list or a prior response, so it goes straight to TLS rather than redirecting. TLS handshake. TCP three-way handshake, then TLS: client hello, server certificate, verification against the certificate store, key exchange, and session resumption via a ticket if one exists. This is expensive, and it is why connection reuse and session tickets matter. HTTP request. Under HTTP/2 or /3 the browser may coalesce requests on one connection. The request carries cookies, Accept, Accept-Encoding, User-Agent, and conditional headers. DNS to edge. Typically a CDN anycast address; TLS terminates at the edge, which serves from cache or forwards. Origin. The CDN forwards to an origin, usually a load balancer, which picks a target by least-connections or least-response-time, with health checks removing dead instances. Application. Middleware in a fixed order: helmet → CORS → request id → body parse → auth → rate limit → route → error handler. Data. The handler calls a service, which calls a repository: one query, one pooled connection, cached if appropriate. Response. Status, headers (Cache-Control, Vary, security headers, cookies), and a body, with compression negotiated via Accept-Encoding. Rendering. HTML parses; render-blocking CSS and parser-blocking JS are handled; first contentful paint; then hydration, then async chunks. Sub-resources and feedback. Images, fonts, deferred JS; hydration makes it interactive; an SPA route change then needs no network round trip.

questions.text: Explain the JavaScript event loop, microtasks, and why setTimeout(fn, 0) runs last. 🟢 Beginner · Must-know
questions.answer: JavaScript has one call stack and queues of work. The loop: take the next macrotask, run it to completion — draining the entire microtask queue after each task and after each microtask — render, then repeat. Macrotasks: setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI events, MessageChannel, postMessage. Microtasks: promise then/catch/finally, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver. So setTimeout(() => log(1), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => log(2)); log(3) prints 3, 2, 1: log(3) is synchronous, log(2) runs when the stack empties (before the next macrotask), and log(1) waits for a fresh tick. The delay is not magic — setTimeout(…, 0) enters a task queue, and nested timeouts are clamped to ~4ms after five levels.

questions.text: useEffect dependencies: what is compared, and what is the trap? 🟡 Intermediate · Must-know
questions.answer: The dependency array is compared element-wise with Object.is between renders. A length change always re-runs. No array means every render; an empty array means once after first render. The traps: Stale closures. [] closes over the first render's values forever. Fix: include what you read — or better, stop reading it. Use the functional updater (setState(prev => …)), a useRef for a value that should not retrigger, or move the read into the event handler. Objects and functions in the array. [{a: 1}] is a new object each render, so the effect re-runs every render. Memoise it, destructure the primitives you read, or compute inside. Development double-invocation. StrictMode intentionally mounts, unmounts, and remounts in development; a non-idempotent effect or a missing cleanup shows it. Fix: make every effect idempotent and clean it up properly, because production also remounts on Suspense boundaries and navigations. Effects that fetch on mount. Every caller must then guard. Prefer a data-fetching library that owns caching, or move the fetch to a route loader.

questions.text: When is an index not used? Give five reasons. 🟡 Intermediate · Must-know
questions.answer: A function or expression on the column. WHERE date(created_at) = '2026-01-01' cannot use a plain index. Fix: an expression index, or rewrite to a sargable range created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-01-02'. Implicit type conversion. WHERE user_id = '42' on an int column may cast the column. Match the parameter type. A leading wildcard. LIKE '%son' cannot use a B-tree. Fix: trigram or full-text index, or an exact prefix. The query returns a large fraction of rows. At 40% a sequential scan is cheaper than index lookups plus heap fetches; the planner is right, and "fixing" it makes it slower. A union branch whose type does not match the indexed column. The planner may take the branch without the index. (Bonus) Stale statistics. After a bulk load, ANALYZE has not run and estimates are wrong — a common cause of a "suddenly slow" query.

questions.text: Design a rate limiter. 🟡 Intermediate · Must-know
questions.answer: Two phases: the algorithm, and the state.

questions.text: Explain refresh token rotation with reuse detection. 🟡 Intermediate · Must-know
questions.answer: A 15-minute access token plus a long-lived refresh token in an httpOnly cookie. The access token can live in memory; the refresh token must not be readable by JavaScript.

questions.text: Explain the N+1 problem and three fixes. 🟢 Beginner · Must-know
questions.answer: Fetch 100 posts, then loop and fetch each author: 101 queries for one page. It is the most common ORM trap and usually invisible in development because per-query latency is low and the dataset is small. Three real fixes: Eager load / join. findMany({ include: { author: true } }) generates a join or a second batched query. Verify the generated SQL — that is the actual skill; read the query log. Batch. Extract ids, run one WHERE id IN (…), join in memory with a Map. Works without an ORM and is the safest general fix. DataLoader / a batching layer. For graph traversal it batches all loads for one event-loop tick into one query and caches per request, so a repeated lookup is free.

questions.text: What is idempotency, and where must it hold? 🔴 Advanced · Must-know
questions.answer: Performing an operation N times has the same effect as once. With at-least-once delivery, duplicates will happen, and the alternative is charging someone twice or sending two emails. Where it must hold, easiest to hardest: The API boundary. A client-supplied key persisted with a unique constraint. First request inserts; a retry gets a conflict and you return the *original response*, not an error. Essential for anything a client will retry. Your handlers. A job that runs twice must not send two emails: record the effect in the same transaction as the effect itself, keyed by an idempotency key, and return early on conflict. The external call. Pass a key to the provider (Stripe returns the original object on replay). Where a provider offers no idempotency, use a natural key — your id in their reference field, with a search before create. At-least-once consumers. ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING plus a unique constraint on the natural key.

questions.text: How do you run a schema migration with no downtime? 🔴 Advanced · Must-know
questions.answer: Run migrations as a separate one-off step *before* the new version serves traffic, guarded by an advisory lock, and make every migration backward-compatible with the version still running. That second half is what makes a rolling deploy safe, and it is the half people forget.

questions.text: Explain EXPLAIN ANALYZE output and how you read it. 🟡 Intermediate · Must-know
questions.answer: EXPLAIN shows the plan. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes and shows it with real timings and row counts, so never run it on a mutation outside a transaction you can roll back. Read in this order: Estimated versus actual rows per node, and the ratio. A 100× divergence means stale statistics or a predicate the planner did not model — ANALYZE may fix it, or the planner needs help. The loop. A nested loop re-executes the inner side per outer row. actual rows=1 inside an outer node of 500,000 is 500,000 index lookups. loops=. Per-loop cost times the loop count is the real cost. time=0.05 rows=1 loops=900000 is 45 seconds, and this is where people are surprised. Buffers: shared hit=… read=…. Reads are disk, hits are cache. High reads on a hot query mean the working set exceeds shared_buffers. Sort spills — Sort Method: external merge means it went to disk: fix the index or work_mem rather than raising work_mem globally. Node type. Seq Scan is not automatically bad on a small table. Index Only Scan is the target for read-heavy paths and needs a current visibility map or it still visits the heap.

questions.text: Explain retries and why naive retries are harmful. 🟡 Intermediate · Must-know
questions.answer: A naive retry is "try three times on failure". It fails for three reasons: not all failures are retryable (a 400 never succeeds; retrying a validation error is pure waste — retry only 429, 502, 503, 504, and connection errors, and only when the operation is idempotent or carries an idempotency key); retry storms (when a dependency degrades, every client retries at once, and the retries arrive just as it is recovering and knock it over again — this is how a 30-second blip becomes a 20-minute outage); and no jitter (without it, clients that failed together retry together in lockstep, forever).

questions.text: How do you debug a production issue with only logs? 🟡 Intermediate · Must-know
questions.answer: A method, not a vibe: Establish scope. All users, one tenant, one region, one endpoint, one version? Find a failing request id and search on it. If you cannot correlate, that is the finding — add correlation ids. Get a baseline. Error rate, p50/p95/p99, throughput, per-endpoint breakdown, saturation. A problem you cannot scope is usually a change: what deployed, what config moved, which dependency shifted behaviour. Form a falsifiable hypothesis. "The 502s started at 14:02, when the upstream certificate rotated" is testable; "something is wrong" is not. Narrow with data. Does it correlate with a version, tenant, region, status, flag, payload shape, or a particular country (timezones)? Bisect in time. Correlate the first error with deploys, config changes, status pages, and traffic shape. git bisect the deploy range if it looks like code. Reproduce locally with production-shaped data volumes — and say so honestly when a race needing 10k concurrent requests will not reproduce locally. Mitigate first, diagnose second. Roll back, disable a flag, shed load, fail over. The incident is not over until users are unblocked; root-causing during an outage is a privilege, not a duty. Then write it up. Timeline, impact, root cause, contributing factors, and the specific preventive change you shipped. Blameless — the target is the system, not the person.

questions.text: Explain database isolation levels with a concrete anomaly for each. 🟡 Intermediate · Must-know
questions.answer: Four anomalies, each assumed to arise from a transaction that reads then writes: Dirty read — reading uncommitted data. B reads A's uncommitted write; A rolls back; B acted on data that never existed. Postgres Read Committed does not permit this; MySQL InnoDB REPEATABLE READ does not either. Non-repeatable read — the same row read twice returns different values because another transaction committed between. Read Committed permits this, and that is what it means: each statement gets a fresh snapshot. Phantom read — a range query returns different row *sets* because rows were inserted. Postgres snapshot isolation does not permit phantoms within a statement, but two SELECT count(*) calls in one Read Committed transaction can differ. SERIALIZABLE prevents it. Write skew — two transactions read overlapping data, take different decisions, and both commit, breaking a joint invariant. Two on-call doctors each check "at least one is on shift", both see one, both go on break. Snapshot isolation permits it; SERIALIZABLE prevents it by aborting one with a serialization failure, which must be retried. | Level | Dirty | Non-repeatable | Phantom | Write skew | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Read Uncommitted | yes | yes | yes | yes | | Read Committed | no | yes | yes | yes | | Repeatable Read | no | no | mostly | yes | | Serializable | no | no | no | no |

practice.title: K.4 Rapid-Fire Bank
items: Foundations (1–20)
O(1) vs O(log n)? Array indexing is a fixed number of machine operations; a tree descent is one step per level, so it scales with height.
Why is binary search O(log n)? Each comparison halves the search space, so n → n/2 → n/4, reaching 1 in log₂(n) steps.
Amortized O(1) means? The total cost over n operations is O(n) even though individual operations can be O(n) — like doubling a dynamic array.
Hash table worst case? O(n) when all keys collide into one bucket; mitigated by chaining, tree-mode escalation, or randomization.
Stack vs heap allocation? Stack is LIFO, contiguous, automatic lifetime, fast; heap is dynamic, manual/GC lifetime, slower to access.
Process vs thread? A process has its own address space; threads share the heap and file descriptors but have their own stack and registers.
Race condition? Two threads access shared state without synchronization, producing a result dependent on interleaving.
Deadlock requires? Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait — break any one.
Mutex vs semaphore? A mutex is binary ownership of one resource; a semaphore is a counter allowing N concurrent holders.
TCP vs UDP? TCP gives ordered, reliable, congestion-controlled delivery; UDP is connectionless with no guarantees but no head-of-line blocking.
Why head-of-line blocking in TCP? Ordered delivery means a lost segment stalls all later data on the connection.
Three-way handshake? SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK — it synchronizes sequence numbers and establishes the connection state.
Time complexity of Python + on strings? O(n) per append because strings are immutable, so a loop is O(n²); use join.
Bit vs byte? A bit is one binary digit; a byte is 8 bits. Storage is measured in bytes; speed in bits per second.
Encoding vs encryption? Encoding is a reversible representation change (base64, UTF-8); encryption requires a key to reverse.
Big-O vs Big-Theta? Big-O is an upper bound; Big-Theta is a tight bound; Big-Omega is a lower bound.
Recursion → iteration? Use an explicit stack (or queue for BFS), which removes call-stack overhead and the depth limit.
Why is quicksort average O(n log n) and worst O(n²)? Partitioning is linear per level; worst-case pivots give n levels instead of log n.
In-place means? Constant extra space beyond the input — not necessarily O(1) time.
What is a hash collision and how do you handle it? Two keys map to the same bucket; handle by chaining (separate lists), open addressing with probing, or rehashing.
Frontend (21–45)
Event bubbling vs capturing? Events propagate target → ancestors (bubble) or window → target (capture); the bubble phase is the default handler phase.
What causes a reflow? Changing geometry-affecting properties (width, content, position) forces layout recomputation; read-then-write in a loop causes thrashing.
Event loop in the browser? macrotask queue (timers, I/O) → render opportunity → microtask queue (promises) drains completely first.
== vs ===? Loose uses type coercion (null == undefined is true); strict compares type and value.
null vs undefined? undefined means "no value assigned"; null means explicitly "no object/value".
Closure? A function plus the lexical environment it captured when created.
var in a loop with setTimeout? All callbacks see the final value because var is function-scoped; let creates a per-iteration binding.
Hoisting? Declarations are moved to the top of their scope; var becomes undefined, function declarations are initialized, let/const are in the temporal dead zone.
Promise.all vs allSettled? all resolves when all resolve and rejects on the first rejection; allSettled always waits and reports every outcome.
What is a microtask? A job in the microtask queue — promise callbacks and queueMicrotask — drained before the next macrotask.
useEffect dependency array? The values from render that the effect closes over; omitting one gives a stale closure, so include all or restructure.
Why key lists by id? React uses keys to decide which nodes to reuse; index keys misidentify nodes after reorder and corrupt state, focus, and animation.
What does React re-render mean? The component function re-runs and returns a new element tree; React then diffs and commits minimal DOM changes.
useMemo vs useCallback? useMemo caches a computed value; useCallback caches a function identity. Both are for referential stability or expensive work.
What is a render-prop vs hook? A render-prop is a function child receiving data; a hook is a function called inside a component that may use state and effects.
Context vs Redux/Zustand? Context propagates a value; a store adds subscriptions, selectors, and devtools, so only the components that read a slice re-render.
LCP, INP, CLS? Largest Contentful Paint (load), Interaction to Next Paint (responsiveness), Cumulative Layout Shift (visual stability).
How do you fix a large CLS? Reserve space for async content (width/height or aspect-ratio), avoid inserting content above existing content, use skeletons with exact dimensions.

topics.description: Networking within Job Search Strategy.
keyConcepts: The default bridge network has no automatic DNS; container names are not resolvable (legacy --link was the workaround and is obsolete). Any user-defined bridge network gives you DNS for free through the embedded resolver at 127.0.0.11. This is the single most important networking fact: always create a user-defined network for multi-container apps.
Each network is a separate L2 segment with its own subnet; containers on different networks cannot talk by name or IP without routing through the host.
Port publishing vs a real port

-p does not open the container's port on the host. It adds a DNAT rule so traffic arriving at the host port is translated to the container's IP and port. The container's port is only reachable from inside its network namespace and from the host's published address.

Consequences: the container's port number and the host's port number are independent; you cannot publish two containers on the same host port; and the process inside still must listen on 0.0.0.0 (or the specific container IP) for publishing to work — an app bound to 127.0.0.1 inside a container is unreachable from outside, which is a common "why can't I reach it" answer.
Why localhost stops working across containers

Each container has its own network namespace, so 127.0.0.1 is a different loopback in each. localhost is a container-local address, not a service-discovery mechanism. Use the container/service name on a shared user-defined network.

Corollary for developers: localhost:5432 in a container is *that container's* Postgres (nonexistent), not the host's. Use the service name inside a Compose network, or host.docker.internal (Docker Desktop, or --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway on Linux).

The embedded DNS server forwards to the host's resolvers and answers container-name, network-alias, and network-name lookups from Docker's own records. It runs at 127.0.0.11:53 inside the container's netns.
commonMistakes: assuming EXPOSE publishes anything; relying on the default bridge's DNS; hardcoding container IPs; using localhost for a database URL inside a container; publishing to 0.0.0.0 when 127.0.0.1 suffices; --network host "just to debug" and shipping it; assuming the host firewall covers published ports (8.1.6); forgetting that two containers cannot share a published host port.
practiceTasks: build a two-container app (web + API) on a user-defined bridge, prove that name resolution works there and fails on the default bridge, show why localhost fails, add a --network-alias and resolve both names, then attach a third debug container with --network container:web and curl from inside the API's netns.

Your app listens on `127.0.0.1:3000` inside a container and `curl` from the host fails with connection refused. Why, and what are two fixes?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Publishing forwards traffic arriving on the host's published address to the container's IP on the container's port, which only works if something inside the container is listening on a non-loopback address. An app bound to 127.0.0.1 is listening on the container's own loopback interface, and DNAT delivers the packet to the container's eth0 address, so nothing answers and the client gets a connection refusal. Two fixes: bind the app to 0.0.0.0 or to :: inside the container, which is the normal case, and if you want to keep loopback binding, put a reverse proxy in the same container or the same pod. It is the same class of bug as binding to 127.0.0.1 on a VM and wondering why the load balancer cannot reach it."

keyConcepts: Best password hash today? Argon2id, memory-hard, parameters embedded in the hash.
Why Argon2id over bcrypt? Memory-hardness resists GPU/ASIC; scrypt is the fallback; bcrypt's 72-byte limit is a bug source.
Where does the pepper live? KMS or secret store, never in the database or source control.
How do you stop account enumeration at login? One message, one status, and a dummy verify against a fixed hash for unknown users.
What kills the timing oracle? Performing equivalent KDF work on both paths.
Rehash-on-login: why? Spreads a parameter upgrade across real traffic instead of a batch migration.
Per-account vs per-IP rate limit? Per-account is the one that stops distributed credential stuffing; per-IP is trivially distributed.
Account lockout as a DoS? Yes — an attacker permanently locks a victim. Use a soft challenge before a hard limit, and notify.
MFA factors ranked? Passkey/WebAuthn, then TOTP, then backup codes, then SMS, then email.
Why is SMS weak? SIM swap and SS7 attacks make it the attacker's factor.
Passkey advantage? Phishing-resistant — the credential is bound to the origin.
